Pulumi has less community support than Terraform because it is less popular. You can achieve similar results with raw Terraform, which has more documented examples and more people who have already hit and solved the same issues. "I wanted to find Pulumi more useful than I really did."

Used both Pulumi and CDK in depth. Pulumi exposes runtime values to your code, unlike CDK's static templates. Automation API lets you code infra migrations like SQL migrations instead of bash wrappers. Liked Pulumi's resource model, docs, and team responsiveness; now on CDK due to costs but would prefer Pulumi.

People the commenter pitched it to reacted with "Ewww, TypeScript for Infra." For months Pulumi used deprecated Azure stuff and didn't fix it, so "you are always late to the game" compared to plain Terraform. You also need an account with them.

Used to love Pulumi; managing infra plus k8s resources with TypeScript's type system is really nice. However, support responsiveness via Slack and GitHub issues has been poor enough that the team is strongly considering removing it from internal tooling.

Switched from Terraform to Pulumi on a new project because it handles both cloud infrastructure and k8s configuration. Deleting k8s resources everywhere when a config file is removed is otherwise hard.

With a 40k-line Terraform codebase, Pulumi's documented migration paths are "completely intractable." tf2pulumi just spits out a single stream to stdout, which won't work for large projects; auto-generating a project structure from .tf modules and .tfstate would be needed.
"I love Pulumi. It's a joy to use a proper programming language to manage infra."
"Switched from nixops to pulumi, found it much easier to use."
Has used Pulumi for about a year to manage 5+ GCP and AWS environments of around 500 resources each. It was buggy at the beginning, but there was a lot of improvement once typing was added.
Complaint, citing the docs: self-hosting is only available with the Pulumi Enterprise Edition.
The org has banned anything other than Terraform for standardization, so the first barrier is the lack of an HCL-to-Pulumi migration path. "The next big stumbling block is your license..."
Interested in code inlining (function serialization), but it is JS/TS only. Support for Azure Functions is still in its infancy, which holds them back since they're stuck on Azure.
"I really liked Pulumi, but it became too complex after a short while." Defining infra resources procedurally in Python meant struggling to arrange and resolve dependencies.
"I'm in love with Pulumi. Simply one of the best tools I have in my stack." After about a year, the commenter can't go back to editing YAML files or clicking through web UIs.

New to IaC and has used Pulumi for a few months; loves it. The downsides are in the docs, mostly around limits on resource name lengths. Their company runs Pulumi in the CI/CD pipeline of all microservices.
Gave up on Pulumi after discovering it only works by calling into "the mothership," so you cannot build airgapped infrastructure with it.

Ran into Pulumi's two phases (building the DAG, then applying it). Resource attributes like a subnet ID are effectively futures, so you can't use them in conditionals. Using the value required pushing code to be evaluated in the second phase.
"Twice I've tried to love Pulumi but wind up going back to Terraform because the Terraform provider docs put clear usage examples front and center."
Tried Pulumi in private beta and are very happy with it. Having used many tools in this space, it's the first time an engineer told them: "I really like it, I hope we can keep using it."

Alpha tester who liked it so much they added Kubernetes support in their free time. Using a real language makes sharing, dependencies, and transforms much simpler than templating YAML. You can write libraries with secure defaults and use standard dev tools to audit and refactor.
